title: Oedipus at Colonus
author: Sophocles
openingText: Child of an old blind sire, Antigone, What region, say, whose city have we reached? Who will provide today with scanted dole This wanderer? 'Tis little that he craves, And less obtains—that less enough for me; For I am taught by suffering to endure, And the long years that have grown old with me, And last not least, by true nobility. My daughter, if thou seest a resting place On common ground or by some sacred grove, Stay me and set me down. Let us discover Where we have come, for strangers must inquire Of denizens, and do as they are bid.
about:
Oedipus at Colonus is the second of Sophocles's Theban plays in the order of their action — the aged, blind Oedipus arrives at a sacred grove outside Athens, accompanied by his daughter Antigone, looking for the place where he is fated to die. He has been an exile since the events of Oedipus Rex. His sons are at war over Thebes. His brother-in-law Creon has come to claim him for political advantage.

Sophocles wrote the play in his nineties and it was produced after his death in 406 BCE. It is unusual among Greek tragedies in that its action turns toward something like redemption — Oedipus, the most cursed figure in Greek myth, becomes in his death a blessing on the place that takes him in. The play is one of the most beautiful Sophocles wrote.

angleCards.title: Sophocles at ninety.
angleCards.text: This is a valedictory play — written in the last year of a long life, performed after the author's death. Notice where the voice has softened from Oedipus Rex, where the anger has become something more like wonder, and what a playwright chooses to say when he knows this is the last thing he will say.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this as a late work — to trace how Sophocles's voice changed over a lifetime and what he chose to affirm at the end of it.

angleCards.title: Suffering as sanctity.
angleCards.text: Oedipus has done nothing to redeem himself. He has simply suffered, for a very long time. And yet the gods declare his body a blessing to whatever land receives it. The play asks whether endurance itself — without redemption, without moral transformation — can become a kind of holiness.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand what the play is claiming about suffering — whether it can be sanctifying without being deserved or earned.

angleCards.title: Reconciliation, not resolution.
angleCards.text: Oedipus does not forgive his sons. He curses them. He does not make peace with the past — he pronounces on it. This is not a play about healing. Watch how the play distinguishes between resolution (which is impossible) and the stranger thing that actually happens to Oedipus at the end.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this as a study in what comes after tragedy when resolution is impossible — what Sophocles puts in its place.

angleCards.title: Athens and Thebes.
angleCards.text: Theseus and Creon are studies in contrast: the king who keeps his word and the man who does not, the city that offers refuge and the one that uses people. Sophocles is making an argument about political character — written, pointedly, while Athens was losing a war.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the political argument — what Sophocles is saying about Athens and Thebes, hospitality and power, and what kind of city can receive an Oedipus.

cast.name: Oedipus
cast.description: Old, blind, and twenty years in exile, guided by his daughter and carrying nothing but a prophecy. He is no longer the king who solved riddles — he is something harder to name: a man whose ruin has become a kind of power.

cast.name: Antigone
cast.description: Oedipus's daughter, who left Thebes to guide him into exile. She leads him step by step through a world he cannot see, and her loyalty to him is absolute — a loyalty that will cost her everything in Sophocles's earlier play.

cast.name: Ismene
cast.description: Oedipus's younger daughter, who remained in Thebes. She arrives at Colonus as a bearer of news: there is a prophecy about her father's grave, and back home, his sons are at war over the throne.

cast.name: Theseus
cast.description: Ruler of Athens and the play's model of just kingship — a man who gives his word and keeps it without qualification. He receives Oedipus as a suppliant and protects him with his city's full authority.

cast.name: Creon
cast.description: Oedipus's brother-in-law, arrived from Thebes with soldiers and arguments. He needs Oedipus — or his body — for political reasons, and he will use force when persuasion fails.

cast.name: Chorus of Elders
cast.description: The elders of the Attic village of Colonus, guardians of the sacred grove. They are frightened of Oedipus at first — his name is a kind of pollution — and their gradual acceptance of him is the play's emotional spine.

whyItMatters.title: A Late Sophocles, Still Working
whyItMatters.body: The play was written in Sophocles's nineties, when he was the oldest surviving great Athenian tragedian, and concerns an old man at the end of suffering. It is one of the most striking examples in literature of late style — the formal control of long practice, the tenderness of someone who has seen everything.

whyItMatters.title: The Man Who Did Not Choose His Crimes
whyItMatters.body: The play returns to the question Oedipus Rex left unsettled: what is Oedipus guilty of, having done what was prophesied before he was born? Here Sophocles answers more gently. Suffering itself, the play suggests, has reshaped him into someone the gods receive.

whyItMatters.title: The Sacred Stranger
whyItMatters.body: Oedipus arrives in Athens as a stranger, blind, dependent. The Athenians take him in. The play stages, at the end of Sophocles's life, a different vision of his own city: Athens as the place where the broken are received and become a blessing.
